rv.q: Larry David's first foray into Broadway comedy is like watching a weird -- but undeniably entertaining and, God help us all, even potentially transformative -- fusion
By the admittedly exceptional comic standards David has laid down, this ranks alongside an average episode of Curb Your Enthusiasm.

The director, Anna D. Shapiro, moves bodies around the stage with little visible evidence that she’s concerned about their inner lives, and rarely steps outside the Broadway machinery to reënvision the dreck she’s stuck with.
There are plenty of laughs in the play's minor comic questions.
In that respect, Fish in the Dark is more than pretty good, it's pretty great.
It’s well built, occasionally thoughtful, and consistently very funny if not transcendently so.
A half-hour seems just the right amount of time you want to spend with these folks on any given evening.
Many people don't care about the niceties of a well-made play — which this two-act evening is not — they just enjoy seeing a favourite funny man in person.
That kind of low energy smothers comedy.
This is a comedy which, despite the occasional amusing twist, could have been written by someone who hasn't seen a play since the early days of Neil Simon.
David's performance is serviceable but hardly commanding, and his writing feels more like a lengthy television sketch than a fully realized theatrical work.
Others may wonder whether so scattershot a piece of writing would have got this far without its physically rangy, bespectacled star attached.
Imagine a Neil Simon play without a plot—or three bottom-drawer episodes of “Curb Your Enthusiasm” hastily knocked together into a two-hour script—and you’ll get the idea.
It’s a topic that puts David in his element.

"The fish that figures in ads for the new play and can be seen on the drop curtain at the Cort Theater is pretty great, a charming and maddening creature destined to capture your heart. O.K., if you insist: It is pret-ty, pret-ty, pret-ty great. The show for which this fish stands? Not so much...
David's play is competently constructed and has some funny moments, but it feels more like a very long sketch than a fully realized work of theater.
If the result is only pretty good, Curb fans should nevertheless look forward to it with, well, enthusiasm.
Art it ain't; Fish in the Dark isn't O'Neill, or even O. Neil Simon. But it's funny, and it's boffo.

Jayne Houdyshell is terrific as the passive-aggressive mom who gets seduced by a young man (Jake Cannavale, son of Bobby), who's a dead ringer for her dead husband, not knowing he was fathered by her mate when he was cheating on her with the maid (Rosie Perez, doing her Rosie Perez thing).
Over two hours, this “Fish” can feel a bit thin.
So the play is a kind of transfer without transformation.

Whatever the inspiration for “Fish,” devotees of “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm” will not be disappointed, familiar as they are with David’s zingers on the human condition, especially the dubious joys of marriage: “I want to live alone. I just don’t want to die alone.”
If its humor can be predictably caustic, Fish's tone is pleasingly light and flaky.
David's play is pleasant enough, but it feels more like a very long episode of Curb Your Enthusiasm than a fully realized theatrical work.
Hardly a great work of dramatic literature, “Fish in the Dark” hearkens back to the silly and insubstantial Broadway comedies of the 1960s, full of one-dimensional characters and nonsensical farce.
“Fish in the Dark” is the lightest of entertainments, so much so that it’s almost shocking how much deep talent, on stage and behind the scenes, is associated with this show.
David's less original and nuanced play will keep the cash registers ringing as long as he's on stage to dish up the gags.
Then again, they wouldn’t be missing a lot.
Larry David's Fish in the Dark is not a play in any traditional sense, but rather an extended comedy sketch
Most theatergoers, though, will be better off throwing this one back in the river.
“Fish in the Dark” scoops up the yuks.
Fish in the Dark starring Larry David is so bad that the irony of the situation becomes funny.
David's play is a mess: poorly structured, with jokes that don't land and characters that feel like half-formed sketches rather than real people.
And in Anna D. Shapiro's production the actors are all performing in different styles around Mr. David's self absorbed vacuum.
The bottom line – it’s goddamned funny.
All of this amounts to be an exciting, hilarious spectacle that works much more than it doesn’t, with you still not being able to believe that this is actually happening.

Fortunately, the play, which opens tonight, is a worthy outlet for both their cash and their adoration, rewarding audiences with two hours that at their best combine the winning aspects of his signature sitcoms
As a play with plausible characters and story, “Fish in the Dark” is merely tinned TV fare but as a sketchy showcase for David’s brand of brackish comedy, it’s pretty tasty.
It’s bathroom humor, it’s stupid.
But keep in mind, that although this is a tough ticket to score (mostly sold out) you have to be a big time Larry David fan or this won’t work for you.
Was the applause tepid? Reluctant? Polite? Dutiful?
Mr. David aims to please, but the end product is an unsatisfying half-baked comedy.

cn.t: Larry David's Broadway debut draws fans with his signature neurotic humor from "Curb Your Enthusiasm," but critics find it feels more like an extended TV sketch than a fully realized play, with mixed results.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats
